extracted.intended_audience: students, readers, critics and writers of poetry (general educated audience interested in poetic theory and composition)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic and prescriptive guidance on what poetry is, what subject-matter and forms suit it, and how poetic language, passion, imagination, and sound should be deployed; aimed at evaluating and composing poetry. Based on Hazlitt's Lectures on the English Poets (Lecture I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is a natural vivid impression
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best general notion which I can give of poetry is, that it is the natural impression of any object or event, by its vividness exciting an involuntary movement of imagination and passion, and producing, by sympathy, a certain modulation of the voice, or sounds, expressing it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should produce a vivid, involuntary imaginative and passionate response; successful poems create that spontaneous movement in reader/listener and even modulate the voice (sound) to express it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is the language of imagination and the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry is the language of the imagination and the passions. It relates to whatever gives immediate pleasure or pain to the human mind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject-matter should touch immediate feeling—love, fear, pity, wonder, etc.—rather than abstract or merely argumentative topics. Poetry must address what "comes home" to people in general and intelligible shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter must be universally relevant ('comes home')
rubrics_metrics.description: "...for nothing but what so comes home to them in the most general and intelligible shape, can be a subject for poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects that resonate broadly with human feeling/experience rather than narrowly technical, abstruse, or merely factual matters; accessibility in emotional terms is a criterion for poetic suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry requires heightenings of the imagination (not mere description)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Neither a mere description of natural objects, nor a mere delineation of natural feelings, however distinct or forcible, constitutes the ultimate end and aim of poetry, without the heightenings of the imagination."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetry goes beyond accurate description: it intensifies, magnifies, links images, and uses imagination to transfigure objects and feelings (comparison, metaphor, hyperbole). Mere faithful depiction without imaginative elevation is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation of nature incorporating imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry then is an imitation of nature, but the imagination and the passions are a part of man's nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic representation is faithful to human experience insofar as imagination and passion are natural faculties; altering, distorting, or amplifying facts is permissible and often necessary because the mind experiences things through feeling and fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry represents forms and feelings by their suggestive relations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry represents forms chiefly as they suggest other forms; feelings, as they suggest forms or other feelings."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective poems should connect images and emotions so that one impression evokes related images/feelings—associative, suggestive thinking (metaphor, synecdoche, symbol) is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry describes the flowing, not the fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry puts a spirit of life and motion into the universe. It describes the flowing, not the fixed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should capture movement, process, transition and dynamism (progress, suspense, change), rather than presenting static tableaux alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion and exaggeration to achieve sublimity/pathos (especially tragic poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic poetry "strives to carry on the feeling to the utmost point of sublimity or pathos, by all the force of comparison or contrast; loses the sense of present suffering in the imaginary exaggeration of it; exhausts the terror or pity by an unlimited indulgence of it..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for tragic/sublime effects, intensify emotional arcs, use contrasts and escalations, and allow feeling to expand imaginatively—while keeping sympathy (not disgust). Hazlitt illustrates with Lear, Othello.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic exhibition should excite sympathy without disgust
rubrics_metrics.description: "One mode in which the dramatic exhibition of passion excites our sympathy without raising our disgust is, that in proportion as it sharpens the edge of calamity and disappointment, it strengthens the desire of good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage or narrative displays of extreme feeling should be constructed so they deepen audience sympathy and aspiration rather than merely repelling; balance intensity with moral or imaginative framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must appeal to whole human constitution (moral, intellectual, sensitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Impassioned poetry is an emanation of the moral and intellectual part of our nature, as well as of the sensitive--of the desire to know, the will to act, and the power to feel; and ought to appeal to these different parts of our constitution, in order to be perfect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best poetry engages intellect and will as well as feeling: it awakens thought and moral imagination, not only sensory sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic pleasure grounded in love of strong excitement (not anomaly)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure derived from tragic poetry "has its source and ground-work in the common love of strong excitement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are attracted to heightened feeling because of a general appetite for intense experience; poets may exploit this natural appetite ethically and artistically, rather than treating it as pathological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is musical thought: rhythm and harmony must match feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Milton: "Thoughts that voluntary move / Harmonious numbers." Poetry should align thought and modulation of sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verse form (meter, rhythm, cadence) should mirror and enhance the emotional and imaginative movement of content; musicality is intrinsic to poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry supplies harmony missing from prose (sound echoing sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry makes these odds all even. It is the music of language, answering to the music of the mind...to make the sound an echo to the sense..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic collocation of syllables, cadence and other sonic devices so that sound reinforces meaning. When prose's jerks/harshness interrupt reverie, verse should restore a rising sustained musical flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification must suit the subject (blank verse vs rhyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Pope's versification is tiresome, from its excessive sweetness and uniformity. Shakspeare's blank verse is the perfection of dramatic dialogue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a metrical/versification method appropriate to tone and genre: excessive polish/uniformity (e.g., Pope) can deaden effect; blank verse may better serve dramatic, energetic speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme assists memory and may quicken fancy, but can be limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is allowed that rhyme assists the memory...But if the jingle of names assists the memory, may it not also quicken the fancy?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhyme is a tool—useful for mnemonic and playful effects—but beware mechanical or over-sweet rhyming that undermines imaginative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all verse is poetry: content/imaginary power matters
rubrics_metrics.description: "All is not poetry that passes for such: nor does verse make the whole difference between poetry and prose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter alone doesn't make poetry. Works that move the imagination (e.g., Pilgrim's Progress, Robinson Crusoe) may be poetic in effect even without conventional verse; conversely, rhymed verse may still be merely Gazette-like if lacking imaginative depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry vs eloquence/argument: poetry is not for disputable subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote: "The difference between poetry and eloquence is, that the one is the eloquence of the imagination, and the other of the understanding. Eloquence tries to persuade the will, and convince the reason: poetry produces its effect by instantaneous sympathy. Nothing is a subject for poetry that admits of a dispute."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making poetry primarily argumentative or didactic; subjects that invite debate or rely on technical reasoning are better served by eloquence; poetry relies on immediate shared feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets often fail at prose because images don't carry argument
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poets are in general bad prose-writers, because their images, though fine in themselves, are not to the purpose, and do not carry on the argument."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing non-poetic prose, don't rely solely on evocative images; argumentative clarity and logical progression are different competencies than creating poetic images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry suggests what exists beyond the object; painting gives the object
rubrics_metrics.description: "Painting gives the object itself; poetry what it implies."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should aim to evoke implications, associations and progressions rather than merely depict visual detail. For emotional narrative and progress, poetry can be superior to static visual representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry thrives on the unknown and undefined; modern knowledge/civilization limits imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: "The province of the imagination is principally visionary, the unknown and undefined: the understanding restores things to their natural boundaries...the progress of knowledge and refinement has a tendency to circumscribe the limits of the imagination, and to clip the wings of poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imaginative power feeds on mystery and the unquantified; too much literalism, policing of experience, or over-rationalization can diminish poetic possibilities. Use wonder and the unmeasured to enliven poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must 'strike and fix the imagination'—coincidence of image, words, and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the perfect coincidence of the image and the words with the feeling we have...that gives an instant 'satisfaction to the thought.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for moments where language and image exactly embody the felt experience—these produce immediate satisfaction and lasting effect. Strive for apt metaphors and phrasing that feel inevitable.
